arrival.title: 01 / The house with the blue door

lines.text: The bus leaves you with a warm suitcase handle, a mouthful of salt air, and the uncomfortable suspicion that you have arrived on the wrong day of your own life.
The timetable at the stop has changed. The sea has not. Beyond the rooftops, it keeps folding and unfolding itself, utterly occupied.

At twenty-three, you expected returning to feel more like an arrival. Instead you stand outside the gate, looking for somewhere to put your hands. Eight years since you moved away at fifteen; the latch still sits at the same height.
Summerhouse. Your grandmother painted the name herself, then complained for seventeen years about the spacing of the letters.
Someone has recently oiled the gate. It opens without the long, theatrical squeal you were preparing for. Somehow this is the first thing that hurts.
There are six weeks until the handover. Six weeks to sort a house into things to keep, things to give away, things you cannot bear to decide about yet. Your return ticket waits in your email.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: If you’re selling something, we already have a very good collection of things.
Rowan stands on the porch with a screwdriver in one hand and half a door latch in the other. There is a pale crescent of sawdust on his sleeve.
You knew he still lived next door. You had imagined this encounter on the bus, and again at the station. In none of those versions was he holding part of your door.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Hello, {name}.
He says it carefully. As though your name is a glass he has just found at the back of a cupboard.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Hello, Rowan.
At twenty-three, he has the same uncertain smile and a different way of standing: one shoulder braced toward a job that needs doing.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I was going to have this fixed before you got here. As a welcoming gesture. It’s become more of a hostage situation.
You set your case down. The two of you make the same half-step forward, then stop.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: What are we doing? Hug? Handshake? Formal inspection of the latch?

choices.text: “Come here.” Offer him a hug.
“Let’s start with the latch.” Give him a smile.
“I’m glad you’re here. I need a minute first.”

lines.text: Rowan puts the screwdriver down first. The tiny care of it catches you off guard.
His embrace is warm and a little sideways, both of you negotiating your changed heights and the years between you. His shirt smells of clean laundry and wood shavings.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You made it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: The bus driver tried quite hard to prevent that.
Rowan laughs against your shoulder. Then he steps back, letting you be the one to end it.
For a second the porch seems much smaller than it used to. Or perhaps you no longer need as much room to stand in it together.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Excellent. A shared enemy.
He turns the latch so you can see a tiny spring sticking out at an accusatory angle.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Is that supposed to be outside it?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: In a philosophical sense, who can say?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: In the door sense.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: No.
The laugh comes out of you before you can organize it. Rowan’s shoulders lower a fraction. He doesn’t try for the hug again.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Of course. Gate’s open. No timetable.
He sits on the porch step and begins fitting the spring into the latch. It gives you something to look at that isn’t his face.
You stand under the jasmine until the smell stops feeling like a memory and starts being a smell again.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Okay. I think I can come in now.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Good. I was about to ask you to hold this screw. Very demanding reunion, honestly.
He puts it in your palm. One small, manageable thing.
The hall is cool. Linen curtains lift at the open window and settle against the sill with a sound like someone turning a page.
Your grandmother’s weather station still hangs beside the door: a pine cone suspended from string. Beneath it, her label reads EXTREMELY ADVANCED EQUIPMENT.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Does it work?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Better than my phone. Less advertising.
Your suitcase catches on the same raised floorboard. You apologize to it automatically.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: She kept meaning to get that fixed.
You look down. There is a neat pencil mark beside the board, and a date from last autumn.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I kept meaning to fix it.
He takes your case upstairs before you can think of an answer. You listen to his footsteps: he knows which stairs complain.
On the kitchen counter there are three labeled tins. TEA. BISCUITS. NOT BISCUITS. The last contains screws.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: A deeply unfair system.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: It was more of a warning than I usually got.
He returns with an empty tray and begins opening cupboards. His ease here is useful. His ease here is also something you weren’t ready to see.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I can show you where things ended up. Or leave you to it. I took today off, but that doesn’t make me part of the inventory.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You took a day off?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: The chandlery will survive without me selling someone the wrong size washer for one afternoon.
There is room in the offer for you to refuse it. You are grateful for that room.

choices.text: “Stay. I could use someone who knows where to start.”
“Stay, but I get to be useless for the first hour.”
“I want to do some of this myself. One room together?”

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: One room together. And you get the final say. It’s your house to sort.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Uselessness approved. I’ll put it on the rota.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Then I’ll stay. We can start with something small.
You agree on the little room facing the sea. It used to be yours in the summers, then a storeroom, then apparently a battlefield between bed linen and cardboard boxes.
Rowan opens a window. His brown hair is tied in the same low bun, a loose strand catching on his earring. Somewhere below, a neighbor is trying to persuade a dog to surrender a gardening glove.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We need a system.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Keep, donate, and deeply mysterious?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You’ve done this before.
The first box contains travel adapters, a broken egg timer, and eleven postcards from the same woman in Norwich. None mentions Norwich.
You read one aloud. It describes an exceptional pear.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Good for her.

Rowan lifts an old illustrated book from the box, holding it open while you inspect its penciled captions. Under it is the guest register. Your grandmother’s handwriting narrows on busy weekends, then grows enormous whenever she is annoyed.
One entry says: LOVELY FAMILY. CHILD PUT SOAP IN PIANO. DISCUSS.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Was that us?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I would remember being a lovely family.
You spend a while making separate piles. Rowan asks before moving anything from yours. Even the dead batteries.
Behind the spare blankets, you find a faded beach towel. A corner is stitched with crooked green thread. You remember hiding here during thunderstorms, making rooms inside rooms.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: What did we call our headquarters? I remember having to knock. Even though it was a towel.
You can almost hear your younger voice issuing instructions. The exact place comes back with it.

choices.text: The linen cupboard: a very exclusive ship.
Under the kitchen table: our secret radio station.
The garden shed: headquarters for lost things.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: It was {hideout}. We took the security arrangements very seriously.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Right. And your grandmother would announce herself as a delivery of emergency toast.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: She knew the password.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: She invented the password. It was “toast.”
You both laugh. Outside, the dog has apparently won. A person says, with considerable feeling, “Fine. Keep it.”
Rowan folds the towel instead of putting it in either pile.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I remember it being quieter. In there, I mean. Even with you doing all the voices.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I did excellent voices.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You did one voice. It was a mayor.
The towel goes on the bed. You let the quieter part of what he said remain beside it, without pulling at the thread.
In the desk drawer you find a tin pencil case. It rattles. There is a small blank label on top, waiting for a name.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: What was the thing you kept in there? The thing nobody was allowed to touch without filling out a form?

choices.text: A blue marble that “predicted” the weather.
A bus ticket from our first solo trip into town.
A shell shaped, approximately, like a dragon.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: It was {treasure}. Obviously priceless.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Obviously. Shall we call a museum or just the police?
Inside the pencil case is exactly that. Smaller than you remember. An empire’s worth of importance, fitting in your palm.
For a little while you tell Rowan why it mattered. Your story takes a turn you didn’t expect: you remember wanting something ordinary to be proof that an extraordinary day had happened.
Rowan doesn’t laugh at that part.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I think it worked.
You set it on the windowsill. Light moves through the old glass, wavering over your hand.
Under the drawer liner is a photograph of two sunburned children standing beside a sandcastle that seems to consist entirely of a moat.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: A bold architectural direction.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We ran out of castle.
On the back, your grandmother has written: {name} says {subject} should be in charge. Rowan has requested a recount.
There is another word underneath, in your own enormous handwriting. Your self-appointed title, used for one entire summer.

choices.text: “Captain.” I was responsible for navigation. Badly.
“Professor.” I knew several facts about crabs.
“Trouble.” Grandmother made that one official.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: {nickname}. That’s right. I had to put that on your birthday card.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You could have applied for a promotion.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I preferred being someone the coastguard couldn’t prosecute.
When you lift the photograph, a folded sheet slips out behind it. Green ink shows through the paper. You recognize the color before the words.
You used to fight over that pen. It smelled of apples, theoretically. Mostly it smelled of a pen someone had put near an apple.
The heading says BEFORE WE GET BORING. You were both twelve when you wrote it. Beneath it, in two competing styles of handwriting, is a list.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Watch the sunrise from the old pier.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Perform a song in front of someone.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Tell each other a secret. Take a trip with no planned destination.
Neither of you reads the last line immediately.
Leave town together someday.
The final word is underlined twice. One line is yours. One is his.
You remember packing for the city. You remember intending to call from the station. You remember that there were always other things you were about to do.
Rowan smooths one corner of the paper with his thumb.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We really thought growing up would be mostly transport.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: And public performance, apparently.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: A terrible combination. Bus karaoke.
The joke gives you both somewhere to stand. But Rowan leaves his thumb on the last line.

choices.text: “I wish we’d done more of it before I left.”
“Do you still want any of these?”
“We don’t owe our younger selves everything.”

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Me too.
He says it without a smile, and without trying to make you feel worse. It is an answer, not a verdict.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I kept thinking there would be another summer.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: There usually was. Until there wasn’t.
For a moment you expect him to mention the calls you missed, or the funeral, when everyone spoke to you as if your train home were already arriving.
Instead he moves a glass away from the paper so it won’t leave a ring.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We don’t have to repair all of that this afternoon.
You nod. It is a kindness, but not an eraser. You find you prefer it that way.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Some of them.
He looks out of the window. Across the lane, a line of washing shifts as though everyone inside the clothes has taken one careful step.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I still want to go somewhere I haven’t already given directions to.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That sounds achievable.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes. I’m very good at wanting achievable things for an unreasonable amount of time.
You don’t know yet whether you’re allowed to ask why. Rowan taps the first line before you decide.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: This one’s local. Terrible hours, though.
Rowan looks up, a little quickly.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: No. I suppose we don’t.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I don’t mean it didn’t matter. I mean we get to choose now, too.
He thinks about that. You resist the urge to fill the pause with an easier answer.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: That’s fair. I was about to make this into homework, wasn’t I?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You always did like a checklist.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I like knowing what happens next. Different problem.
His smile is brief, but it reaches you. The paper lies between you, still important and no longer an instruction.
Your stomach makes a noise so decisive it seems to conclude the discussion.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Motion to adjourn.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Seconded.
You tuck the list into the guest register for safekeeping. In the corner, a box labeled KITCHEN contains only lampshades. You decide this can remain tomorrow’s problem.
Rowan finds your keys on the bed and holds them out, then pauses.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: The little brass one sticks. Turn it back a bit before you pull.
You know this. You used to know this. You take the keys without saying either thing.
Outside, the afternoon has brightened. The lane smells of warm stone and somebody’s laundry powder.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: There’s still the chip shop. New owner. Same argument about whether vinegar counts as a vegetable.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: It doesn’t.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You’ve changed.
The high street is both shorter and longer than you remember. Shorter between shops. Longer in all the places where a shop has gone.
The old newsagent is a pottery studio now. A bowl in the window costs more than your childhood bicycle.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Before you ask, I don’t understand the bowls either.
At the chip shop, Rowan orders and then stops before ordering for you.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Same as before? Or has adulthood changed your position on peas?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I’d like to retain the right to evolve.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Brave. Expensive. They charge extra for peas.
You take your paper parcels to the sea wall. The stone is warm through your clothes. Out in the harbor, a boat turns so slowly it seems to be changing its mind.
Rowan digs wooden forks from a pocket, along with a washer, a receipt, and a pencil worn almost to nothing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you have an entire workshop in there?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Only the portable department.
A gull lands three feet away. It has the look of a regular customer disappointed by the service.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Absolutely not.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Don’t establish eye contact. It’ll think you’re management.
You try eating while looking professionally unavailable. The gull advances.

choices.text: “We stand together. Guard the chips.”
“Your noble sacrifice will be remembered.” Protect your own lunch.
Move the parcels under cover. “I believe in diplomacy.”

lines.text: You and Rowan close ranks around the parcels, a united and faintly greasy front.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Betrayal. In front of witnesses. Feathered witnesses.
You tuck both parcels beneath the shelter. Rowan salutes your commitment to conflict resolution.
For a glorious second, your strategy works. Then a second gull arrives from a direction neither of you has been monitoring.
Rowan makes a noise that you have never heard from a person repairing a door.
One chip is taken. No lives are lost. Your dignity remains unaccounted for.
You relocate beneath the shelter, laughing too hard to be discreet. Rowan shakes vinegar from his wrist.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We used to be better at this.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: We used to have adult supervision.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We are the adult supervision.
You consider that in silence.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Someone should be told.
The laughter fades comfortably. Rowan offers you the crispiest chip from his parcel, with the solemnity of a treaty.
His hands have small marks you don’t remember. A scar at one knuckle. A line of blue paint beside a thumbnail.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What do you do when you aren’t fighting doors?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Sometimes I fight boats. For money.
You wait. He looks sideways at you, then relents.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I’ve been trying to build a guitar. There’s a course up north. Instrument making. Proper benches. People who know what they’re doing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you applied?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I’ve developed a very sophisticated relationship with the application page.
He folds the empty corner of his chip paper into a tiny square.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: It’s a year away. Next intake. There’s time.
There is the smallest defensive edge to it. You recognize someone putting a thing back on a shelf where it can’t be broken.

choices.text: “You sound like you really want it.”
“Time can turn into a very comfortable excuse.”
“Want company while you look at the application?”

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I do.
His answer is unexpectedly plain.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I want to make something that doesn’t need me after I’m done. Something a person can take somewhere else and use to make a ridiculous amount of noise.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: That’s a good want.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I think so. It still feels a bit extravagant when I say it out loud.
You finish your lunch without asking him for a plan. Eventually he tells you about tonewoods, and then apologizes for telling you about tonewoods.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I asked.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Dangerous precedent, {nickname}.
Rowan’s paper stops moving.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: It’s not only an excuse. There are things here that need doing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I know. I’m not saying it’s easy. I just heard myself say “there’s time” for years.
Wind lifts a receipt between your shoes. Rowan catches it before it reaches the road.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I don’t like that you might have a point.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You don’t have to like it right away.
He looks at you again. This time his smile is less defensive.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: All right. Ask me about the application again. Another day. I might still be annoying about it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I have experience.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Maybe. Not if it turns into you doing it for me.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I was imagining sitting nearby and criticizing the website.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: There is a lot to criticize.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Then I am qualified.
He unfolds the square of paper he was making, smoothing it against his knee.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Thank you. Let me ask when I’m ready.
You agree. It feels good to offer something with a handle he can choose to take.
At the corner, the lane back to Summerhouse slopes inland. The promenade bends the other way toward the old pier.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We could check whether the pier is still standing. For planning purposes. Or go back. You did travel today.
Your feet are tired, but the afternoon has become the kind you used to resent being called indoors from.

choices.text: Take the longer walk. Ask about his music.
Head home together. Enough adventures for one afternoon.

lines.text: The pier is still there. Narrow, stubborn, and only slightly less straight than the horizon. Fresh boards interrupt the old ones like patches on a favorite coat.
Rowan puts a hand on the railing. You notice that he tests it before leaning.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Do you still play?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Guitar? Yes. Badly, but with considerable persistence.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You used to know three chords.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Four now. I don’t want success to change me.
Below you, water clicks against the pilings. A loose rope taps a mast in the harbor, almost keeping time.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: She used to ask me to play in the kitchen. Your grandmother. While she did the accounts.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I didn’t know that.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Mostly to stop me trying to fix her calculator. It wasn’t broken. She just didn’t believe it.
He looks out at a marker buoy. The small smile stays, even as something else arrives beside it.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I liked having an audience who would tell me when I was terrible.
You stand together until the wind begins to get through your sleeves. Rowan points to the eastern breakwater, where the sun will come up.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Best seat in town. If you ignore the complete absence of a seat.
On the way back, he matches your pace without making a thing of it.

homeward.title: A shorter way is still a way

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Good call. I was trying to look more energetic than I feel.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: We can both retire from that immediately.
You stop at the little grocery for bread. Rowan remembers the milk only when you reach the till and returns with two kinds, so you can choose.
The walk uphill is companionable. No one tries to make it an event.
At the gate Rowan takes the heavier bag. You let him. Then you hold the door while he negotiates the repaired latch.
It is possible, you think, to be looked after without surrendering the whole day.
In the kitchen, evening light reaches halfway across the table. You open a bread bin and find a recipe card tucked under the lid.
LEMON CAKE. Your grandmother’s handwriting. Then, underneath: MORE LEMON THAN THAT.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Very precise.
Rowan looks over your shoulder.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I made it once. Used the amount she told me. She said I’d been timid.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Did you make it again?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes. She said it was aggressive.
The kettle begins its low grumble. Rowan takes cups from the cupboard, setting them out without looking.
One by the window. One near you. One at the head of the table.
His hand stops over the third cup.
It is the yellow one. A crack runs through the glaze under its handle. You used to turn it away from her because you were afraid it would break.
The kettle clicks off. The refrigerator keeps humming. Somewhere upstairs a door moves against its latch.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Sorry.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You don’t have to—
You stop. You don’t know which of the many things you mean should finish the sentence.
Rowan turns the cup once, keeping both hands around it. His thumbnail finds the crack.

choices.text: Sit with him. Let the cup stay for now.
“Tell me about the last time you made her cake.”
“Could we put it away? Just for tonight.”

lines.text: You sit down. After a moment Rowan sits too. The third cup remains where it is, receiving a small square of sunset.
There isn’t a good thing to say. You stop trying to find one.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: She would hate the tea getting cold.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: She’d put it in the microwave and deny it.
Rowan lets out a laugh that doesn’t quite decide what it is. You pour the tea. Only two cups.
For a little while, the ordinary work of passing milk and finding spoons is enough to keep you both at the table.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: She made me take half of it home. Claimed she’d gone off cake.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: She hadn’t.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Absolutely not. I came back the next day and she asked where the rest was.
You laugh, then cover your mouth for no reason you can name.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: It’s all right.
He doesn’t say what is all right. Laughing, maybe. Or not knowing what to do with your hands.
You put the recipe card between you. There is a thumbprint of flour in one corner. Neither of you brushes it away.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yes. Of course.
He returns the cup to the cupboard, carefully enough that it makes no sound.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I’m not trying to pretend.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I know. It’s a lot all at once.
He closes the cupboard and leaves his hand on the knob for a second. You pour his tea while he’s turned away.
When he sits down, you slide it toward him. He nods, accepting the small exchange.
The place at the head of the table is empty. Tonight, that is enough to be looking at.

absence.title: Different versions of the same house

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I used to come over after closing. Check the gutters, move the bins. She paid me in food I hadn’t asked for.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: She told me everything was fine.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: She liked having good news for you.
You look at the pencil mark on the floorboard. From this side of the room, you can see a second mark, half rubbed away.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I thought she meant it.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Sometimes she did.
He turns his spoon over. For a moment you think he will stop there.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Sometimes she was tired. Sometimes I was. I should have told you more.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: I could have asked better questions.
Neither statement cancels the other. The tea is strong. You drink it anyway.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: This was the place I could come when next door was… loud. She never made me explain before she fed me.
You remember your grandmother putting another potato in the pan. You thought she simply liked making too much.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Sorry. That makes it sound like every day was awful. It wasn’t. I had good things, too.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You don’t have to make it one kind of story.
He looks at you then. Properly, for a second.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Neither do you.
Your phone is in your pocket. On it is a voice message from your grandmother, saved in February. Twenty-three seconds. You have not been able to press play since the funeral.
You don't play it now. Having the option is already more than you can hold alongside this kitchen.
Instead, you wash the cups. Rowan dries. You find you still know how to pass him things without looking.
Afterward you bring the promise list down. The green ink has faded most where the paper was folded.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: What time would we have to leave? For the first one.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Four forty. If we want the whole thing.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: There’s a four forty in the morning?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: An administrative error. Unfortunately they kept it.
You rest the paper on the table. The first line feels different from the last. Small enough to put a real time beside.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: We can aim for tomorrow. And if you don’t sleep, we can aim for another day. A promise isn’t a trap.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Bring a flask?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Already mentally bringing a flask.

choices.text: “Tea. Strong enough to negotiate with the morning.”
“Coffee. I need an unfair advantage.”
“Cocoa. We’re allowed one childish decision.”

numbers.title: A way to reach each other

afterchat.title: What a promise can look like

You set the alarm and turn your phone face down. Tomorrow has acquired a time, a place, and someone bringing a flask.
The house makes a settling sound. You used to think it was breathing. Tonight you let yourself think that again.
Before bed, you go looking for a spare pillowcase. The bottom drawer catches on something. You ease it open rather than pulling.
Inside is an exercise book, swollen at the corners. On its cover, in Rowan’s handwriting: THINGS WORTH TELLING {name}.
You remember now. Not one of the five big promises. A small one made {hideoutPlace}, on the last night before you moved away.
You had been afraid you would stop knowing the place. That everyone would continue without you and you would return as a visitor.
Rowan had said, “I’ll save you a bit.” You thought he meant a shell, perhaps. A photograph. You had said you’d do the same.
The first page describes a dog stealing a whole baguette. There is an unconvincing drawing of the dog.
The next page has a bus ticket taped to it. Then a pressed flower. Then a note about the newsagent closing, with its final sweet wrapper tucked beneath.
Years of entries. Not every day. Sometimes months apart. Enough to show that after a gap, he began again.
Near the end, you find: She laughed at the aggressive lemon cake. Properly laughed. Wanted to tell you while I still remembered the sound.
You sit on the floor with the drawer open against your knee.
He hadn’t stopped living while you were away. He had kept a place where he could tell you about it.
Between the final two pages is a loose note in your grandmother’s hand. Rowan said to keep this here. In case you came home when he was out.
You hold the book closed for a moment. Outside, Rowan’s light goes dark.
The list downstairs contains five things unfinished. Up here is a promise that has been quietly happening all along.

I don’t move.
Mom comes over and puts an arm around my shoulders.
I go stiff.

lines.speaker: Mom
lines.text: We’re trying to help you.
I look at the fire.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Please don’t.
Her arm falls away.

lines.speaker: Mom
lines.text: Go upstairs, {name}.
This time, I do.
I take the yellow envelope with me.
After that, whenever I thought about contacting Rowan, I remembered the box.
I was afraid of another argument.
And I didn’t know how to explain what had happened.
So I kept putting it off.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: {name}?
I blink.
He’s holding his phone out.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You okay?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Yeah. Sorry.
I enter his number.
My hands are steady now.
Mostly.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I’ll send you a message so you have mine.

lines.speaker: Rowan · text
lines.text: It’s Rowan.

lines.speaker: Rowan · text
lines.text: The one who’s still alive.

lines.speaker: Rowan · text
lines.text: The one standing in front of you.

lines.speaker: Rowan · text
lines.text: The one standing in front of you.

lines.speaker: Rowan · text
lines.text: The one standing in front of you.
I let out a small laugh.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Thanks for clearing that up.
He slips his phone into his pocket.
I glance at the tools beside the door.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: So. What were you doing to the lock?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Fixing it. It kept sticking.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Oh.
I look at the hammer, then back at him.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Sorry I shouted at you.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You saw a stranger messing with the door. Fair enough.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’re not a stranger.
His smile softens.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: No.

choices.text: Thanks for fixing it.
Have you been looking after the house?
Want a hand?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Thanks for fixing it.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: No problem. Try it later. You shouldn’t have to fight it anymore.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Have you been looking after this place?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Yeah. Your lola used to ask me to help with little things.
He gathers a few loose screws into his palm.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I kept checking in after.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: You’ve been doing that all this time?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: When I can. I live right there.
He nods toward his house.
Like that explains all of it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Want a hand?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I’m nearly done. You could hold this, though.
He passes me a small tin.
I hold it while he drops the screws inside.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Very technical work.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: You’re doing well.
He puts the tools away.
Then he notices me shifting my bag to the other shoulder.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Want help carrying those in?

choices.text: Thanks, but I’ve got them.
Yeah. Could you take this one?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Thanks, but I’ve got them.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Okay. I’ll get the door.
He picks up his tools and steps aside.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Yeah. Could you take this one?

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: Sure.
He takes the bag I offer him.

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Careful. It’s heavy.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: What did you pack?

lines.speaker: You
lines.text: Apparently everything.
He adjusts his grip.

lines.speaker: Rowan
lines.text: I noticed.
Rowan pushes the door open.
It moves without catching.
I follow him in, then stop.
I thought I knew what I’d find.
The same furniture. The same curtains.
Dust, probably.
But someone has been taking care of this place.
I look around.
Everything is familiar.
And I can’t remember it ever looking quite like this.
